schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set the work's revival in the second year of Darius Hystaspis, driven by the prophetic admonitions of Haggai and Zechariah; Zechariah is the grandson of Iddo, son of Berechiah.
Matthew Henry supplies the fifteen-year suspension and its lesson: the temple is built by prophecy, not secular force, and God's raising up prophets is a sign of mercy in store.
Gill fixes the patronymic — grandson of Iddo, his father Berechiah (Zech. 1:1).
Clarke and Wesley agree Zechariah was Iddo's grandson; Wesley reads the prophesying as a command from God to resume building, with a promise of favour and assistance.

Keil dates the resumption to the sixth month of Darius's second year, building on the foundations of Ezra 3:10; Ellicott warns 'then rose up' implies no prior indifference, only prophetic inspiriting to proceed without Darius's formal leave.

Clarke celebrates the alliance of civil (Zerubbabel), ecclesiastical (Jeshua), and prophetic (Haggai, Zechariah) power; Wesley makes the prophets' help their presence and assurance of success, the fifteen-year stoppage now ended.
Gill reads the leaders' rising as an inward work first — spirits stirred and quickened by the prophets' ministry and the Lord's Spirit.

Keil and Ellicott fix Tatnai as satrap/Pecha of Syria and Phoenicia over Judaea's sub-governor Zerubbabel, Shethar-boznai his secretary; Ellicott ties the builders' boldness to the fall of Smerdis and notes the ch. 4 decree was never expressly revoked.
Matthew Henry: no sooner does the Spirit stir the temple's friends than the evil spirit stirs its enemies — yet these adversaries are of a better temper, making some conscience of truth.
Clarke draws Tatnai's character as mild, judicious, and unprejudiced from his very report; Wesley notes the old officials Rehum and Shimshai were dead or removed.
Gill explains the new officers as replacements for the old, dead or displaced at the new king's accession.

Keil argues 'we said' marks the author as an eye-witness and sharer, the speakers being the Jews; the mismatch of question and answer is mere compression. Ellicott reads it as a statement, not a question, the names sought to fix responsibility.
Clarke would drop the interrogation: 'These are the names of the men who make this building' — the Jews' plain answer to Tatnai.
Gill canvasses the options (builders, scribes, Tatnai's party) and lands, with the rest, on the Jews as speakers.

Matthew Henry reads the eye of God two ways — it both baffled the enemies (seven eyes on one stone, Zech. 3:9; 4:10) and quickened the elders to courage; our eye on God, seeing his on us, keeps us to duty.

Keil sees divine protection in Tatnai's forbearance and corrects a mistranslation of the clause; Ellicott stresses God's influence lay on the Persian officials no less than on the Jews, as the fair letter shows.
Gill takes the watching eye as favour: God smiled on the work, encouraged by Spirit and prophets, and protected the elders. Clarke concurs — his especial providence worked in their behalf.
Clarke: the watchful care of God was upon the elders, who were assured of his favour.

themes: the eye of God upon the elders

schools.summary: Keil marks vv.6-7 as the letter's superscription answering the hostile letter of Ezra 4:9, names the Apharsachites a Persian-devoted garrison, and reads the salutation 'peace in all things'; Ellicott sets the despatch's dispassionateness in striking contrast to the earlier accusation.
Gill weighs whether the Apharsachites were a transplanted nation or a distinct colony under Tatnai's rule, without deciding.
Keil reads the salutation 'all peace' as a wish of peace in every respect, the courteous opening of a document that passes at once to a plain statement of facts.

Matthew Henry contrasts the letter's fairness with the earlier venom: the officials told the king truly, set out the Jews' plea, and let the cause be fairly heard — a fairly stated cause keeps its ground.
Gill notes only that this was the inscription of the letter, the customary superscription to a sovereign.
Matthew Henry: the officials owned the God of Israel 'the great God' above all gods, and reported truly — a temple reared for worship, not a city fortified for war.
Ellicott reads 'the house of the great God' as a solemn tribute, pictures Tatnai impressed on coming from Damascus, and insists the 'walls' are those within the temple, not the city walls.

Gill hears the Jews' own name for God, notes even the heathen owned one supreme God, and marks Judea reduced from kingdom to province; Wesley adds the Samaritans thus far agreed in owning 'the great God.'
Clarke: 'with great stones' shows a very strong and costly building.

themes: the house of the great God
a pagan tribute to Israel's God

schools.summary: Keil reads the officials' aim: to learn who authorised the work and the names of the leading men — those who 'act in the capacity of heads,' not merely stand at the head.
Matthew Henry voices the inquisitors' pressure — 'By what authority... who gave you that authority? Have you that which will bear you out?'
Gill identifies the questioned as the elders of Judea, its responsible chief men.
Keil reads the second inquiry as a means to an exact report — the names of the leading men written up for the king; Ellicott: the chief promoters' names were required to make them responsible.
Gill takes the names to be those of the elders who set the workmen about the task and directed it.

themes: confession from a demand for names

schools.summary: Matthew Henry unfolds the plea: not a local deity but the God on whom all creation depends, so no faction; and a prescription to Solomon's house, raising 'the foundations of many generations' (Isa. 58:12).

Keil renders 'We are His, the servants of the God of heaven and earth,' the house raised many years ago by a great king; Ellicott hears national honour, infidelity, and humiliation confessed in a few pathetic, wholly true words.
Clarke is moved by the 'simple, plain, and ingenuous' confession: servants of God who provoked him and were given into their enemies' hands.
Gill notes only that the answer was returned to the purpose and in the manner following.

themes: servants of the God of heaven and earth

schools.summary: Matthew Henry: the captivity punished their sin, not the triumph of the nations' gods; God suspended their religion for a time but never meant a final period to it.

Ellicott: they own themselves punished by God's sole hand and remind the Chaldeans' overthrowers that they too are his instruments; Keil confirms the causal 'for this reason' and the force of 'destroyed.'
Gill: their idolatries provoked God, which alone explains why the servants of the great God and his own house were not preserved but carried captive.

themes: punished by God, not by idols

schools.summary: Keil ties the decree back to Ezra 1:3 and forward to the vessels of Ezra 1:7, noting Sheshbazzar was made pechah — Zerubbabel's own title in Haggai 1:1.
Matthew Henry: the decree did not merely permit but charged and commanded the building, so the work is obedience to an imperial order still on the books.
Gill explains 'Cyrus king of Babylon' — so styled from the first year he held Babylon, though long king of Persia; the warrant dates from the earliest possible hour.
Keil traces the vessels from Nebuchadnezzar's plunder into the temple of Babylon and back out by Cyrus's hand to Sheshbazzar, made governor of Judah.
Matthew Henry: Cyrus entrusted the vessels to be restored to their ancient place and use, and the Jews had them to show in confirmation of their claim.
Gill fills in the commission — Cyrus made Sheshbazzar governor and ordered him to carry the vessels, build the temple, and set them in it (Ezra 1:7).

Ellicott finds a note of historical truth in the three imperatives without copula, the eager rush of a remembered decree; Keil reads the same rapid form and takes 'in its place' to explain why the vessels are lodged in the house to be rebuilt on its old site.
Matthew Henry rests on 'in his place' — the very site as before — commanded in compassion and in veneration of Israel's God, whom Cyrus owned: 'He is the God.'

themes: three imperatives, a note of truth
a pagan king owns 'He is the God'

schools.summary: Keil says 'from that time until now' does not deny the long stoppage, only leaves its cause unmentioned; Ellicott makes the unfinished, Cyrus-decreed house the very thing that demands the king's investigation.
Matthew Henry admires what the elders omit: no complaint of the former governors' malice — rendering not bitterness for bitterness, giving a reason of their hope with meekness and fear (1 Pet. 3:15).
Gill takes Sheshbazzar to be Zerubbabel, who laid (or ordered) the foundation.
Clarke takes Sheshbazzar for the military officer who led the return, though some say Ezra.

debates.question: Who is the Sheshbazzar who laid the foundation?

sides.position: Zerubbabel, under whose hand or order the foundation was laid
the military officer who conducted the people from Babylon (some say Ezra)

schools.summary: Keil describes the request to search the archives (the 'house of the rolls,' Ezra 6:1) for Cyrus's decree; Ellicott: all turned on the original decree, which no act of the usurper could cancel, and which a preserved copy would supply.

Clarke praises the letter's good sense and candour — no passion or prejudice — and sees God's continued regard for a disobedient people, punished in justice, spared in mercy; Wesley: had Artaxerxes heard the cause so fairly, he would hardly have hindered it, for God's people are persecuted only when belied.
Matthew Henry: God's people could not be baited if not dressed in bears' skins — let the cause of God and truth be fairly heard, and it keeps its ground.
Gill explains the treasure house as the archive where the state's laws, decrees, and proclamations were kept for recourse.

themes: the decree certain to be found
